fixes.explanation: An army is not the plan Jesus describes. He says the Son of Man "did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many." (Matthew 20:28). No army and no throne in that sentence. I think that's why it stops people in their tracks.

Levites? Friend, that answer walked into the bakery, looked around, and walked right back out. Jesus says the chief priests and scribes will deliver Him over to the Gentiles (Matthew 20:19). The Gentiles are who He names next, so that's the word that fits the blank.

Galilee isn't what Jesus says here. His words are, "…on the third day He will be raised to life." (Matthew 20:19). The third day is about being raised, not about a travel plan. I'd say that's a pretty big difference from a trip.

No hiding in what Jesus says. He tells the Twelve, "…on the third day He will be raised to life." (Matthew 20:19). That's what He says happens on the third day, and there's no wilderness in it. Raised to life is the answer, baker.

"We can," the brothers answer (Matthew 20:22). Jesus had asked if they could drink the cup He was going to drink. I think they had no idea how big that cup was. Jesus follows up and says they will indeed drink His cup (Matthew 20:23).
They don't ask for more time, friend. The brothers answer, "We can" (Matthew 20:22). That's a plain yes to Jesus' question about the cup. "Not yet Lord" just isn't in the text.

It's the other way around, friend. Jesus tells them, "You will indeed drink My cup…" (Matthew 20:23). So the cup does come to the brothers. About the seats, He says that sitting at His right or left is not His to grant.
Father, right on the money. Jesus says, "These seats belong to those for whom My Father has prepared them." (Matthew 20:23). So it's the Father who has prepared them, and Jesus says so plainly.

Indignant is the word. The ten "…were indignant with the two brothers." (Matthew 20:24). That means they were stirred up and not happy about what was asked. The request came from the mother of Zebedee's sons, and the ten were indignant with her sons.

Pleased is not how the ten took it. The text says they "…were indignant with the two brothers." (Matthew 20:24). They weren't clapping for anybody. I bet it's hard to hear a request like that made about someone else.

Patient would have been nice, but that's not what the text says. The ten "…were indignant with the two brothers." (Matthew 20:24). Indignant means they were upset about it. That's the word to hold onto.

That's it, and it's the heart of the whole passage. Jesus says the Son of Man came "…to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many." (Matthew 20:28). Right before that, He says whoever wants to become great among them must be their servant.
